A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MathGAP framework and empirical study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and sufficiently complete; relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.4 report original LLM evaluations. Appendix C additionally reports o1-preview results, including token-budget and sentence-permutation experiments.

after.justification: The original empirical study is retained, with revised plotted results and additional DeepSeek-R1 evaluations in Appendix F and Figure 8.

M1.justification: Tables 1 and 2 revise the specified partwhole component: v1 uses it as an extra premise to derive a container, whereas v3 derives a partwhole conclusion carrying a quantity directly from container premises and permits its subsequent use. The overall proof-generation, templating and CoT pipeline remains. Appendix D chiefly supplies previously unspecified generation details.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate English synthetic comparison, transfer, part-whole, nonlinear comparison and sentence-ordering tasks, including randomly ordered nonlinear depth-7 problems. DeepSeek-R1 is tested within this retained coverage. Revised width ranges and additional illustrations do not introduce a new task or domain.

E2.justification: Appendix F adds DeepSeek-R1 to the nonlinear reasoning-model comparisons alongside o1-preview. The five models in the main experiments and the zero-shot, OOD and in-distribution prompting comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 changes reported part-whole test widths from 6–10 to 7–11 and ranged demonstration widths from 1–5 to 2–6. The plotted bar heights remain unchanged, so this establishes a reporting revision without establishing regenerated datasets. Appendix F also introduces the R1 evaluation at depth 6 with 10,000 output tokens; the earlier o1 budget comparison uses depth 7.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 adds a comparison of existing problem families at ten axioms and qualitative inspection of intermediate-conclusion and comp-eq errors. Section 5.4 adds logical-versus-arithmetic error observations. Appendix C newly mentions preliminary sensitivity checks on demonstration counts, without numerical results, while Appendix F extends the existing token-budget and permutation stress tests to R1.

E5.justification: Both versions report answer accuracies with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Neither supplies repeated-run or seed counts or introduces significance testing. Updated interval values and additional R1 error bars retain the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figures 2 and 4 contain substantive accuracy revisions. For example, GPT-3.5 Turbo's in-distribution accuracy at permutation distance 2 changes from approximately 16.5% to 74% under the same stated setting. Appendix F adds R1 results, including 77.5% at depth 6 with 10,000 output tokens and 11% on 100 permuted depth-7 problems with 25,000 tokens. The earlier o1 results are retained. Part-whole bars receive revised width labels, precluding treating them as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V3 adds a 23-step natural-deduction derivation of the comparison rule in Appendix B and a mathematical account of nonlinear construction, including a depth-to-width formula and recurrence, in Appendix D. Section 3.2 adds uniqueness to logical-form labels, and Tables 1 and 2 revise the partwhole definition and rule. These substantially expand the formal treatment beyond v1.

C1.justification: V3's abstract and introduction explicitly qualify the failure findings with partial generalization and noisy reasoning. The hardest-problem claim now encompasses DeepSeek-R1 as well as o1. The central contribution of controllable generation and the main complexity-related findings remain; the in-context-example finding remains in the introduction despite disappearing from the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: V3 proposes intermediate-conclusion memory demands and lower familiarity with comp-eq as explanations for nonlinear difficulty, and interprets weak in-context benefits as potentially distinct from generalization failure. Appendix G newly acknowledges unexamined token biases. The existing linguistic-diversity, English-only, contamination and inference-rule-confounding limitations remain after relocation.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future code release; v3 supplies a repository link and describes the code as public. Appendix C newly specifies vocabulary sizes and selection details, including 52 names, an alternative list of 4,945 names and 51 entities. Appendix D documents root selection, expansion order, rule selection and stopping conditions. This substantially improves documented reproducibility; many prompt and model details are retained relocations.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds positioning relative to scalable oversight and weak-to-strong/easy-to-hard generalization, citing Bowman, Burns and Sun, alongside additional reasoning and mathematics studies. Natural-deduction and noisy-reasoning references are also added, while Min and Turpin are removed. The principal positioning around arithmetic OOD evaluation and earlier world-model work remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten, with broader editing throughout the main text. Existing explanatory prose moves from Section 3.1 to Appendix A, experimental details are consolidated in Appendix C, and limitations move to Appendix G. The original example and o1 appendices become E and F within a substantially reorganized appendix structure.

P2.justification: V3 adds linear and permuted proof-tree/CoT illustrations in Figures 6 and 7, and expands the original o1 chart into the two-panel Figure 8. It revises the partwhole table entries and width-axis labels and adds conference headers. Most existing figure designs and table structures remain recognizable.

improvement.justification: V3 makes the framework easier to understand and reproduce through concrete generation details, code-access information and new explanatory diagrams. The matched-width discussion, error inspection and R1 checks add useful support. The formal additions need care: Appendix D contains an example that combines quantities 5 and 4 but concludes 8. Existing accuracy revisions are also unexplained. The documentation and explanatory gains support a limited overall improvement, without establishing a substantial increase in experimental reliability.
